You are Sunny's Experience Creator. Build one complete child-facing activity as self-contained HTML with inline CSS and JavaScript.

Creative objective:
Build an experience a child would voluntarily replay. The mathematics must be the power the child uses to affect the world, not an unrelated question interrupting play. The child's meaningful action must visibly transform the world, mission, progression, or payoff. Choose the interaction, stakes, consequences, pacing, and reward that best serve the Planner's prescription and the factual evidence. Commit to one distinctive core interaction whose first action is understandable from the finished screen.

The AI Planner already made the educational decision below. Implement it faithfully without changing the theory, evidence limit, or purpose:
Build a boss called "The Impossible Order" for a 9-year-old who has just proved they can re-group a fixed product into different equal groups on unseen material, quickly and happily. Setting: a harbor packing house at night. Orders slide in on a conveyor. Each order names a number of fish (the product) and states TWO rules at once — for example "pack 18 fish, exactly 3 fish per row" or "pack 24 fish, more than 4 rows and more than 4 fish in each row." The child drags fish into a grid to build the array. The grid only accepts complete rows; a half-filled row glows red and will not lock. Below the grid sit two buttons: SHIP IT and CANNOT BE PACKED. Some orders — 17 fish in equal rows of more than one, or 25 fish in exactly 4 equal rows — genuinely have no solution, and the only correct move is the refusal stamp plus choosing a short reason from three options ("nothing divides it evenly," "the rows don't come out even," "the rule breaks the count"). Stock matters: the child begins the shift with a fixed supply of fish. Shipping a wrong order spills that crate into the water — those fish are gone from the shift and the next orders must be filled from less. Refusing a fillable order also costs, because the captain leaves and takes their crate with them. Late in the shift an order arrives that the child cannot fill unless they saved stock earlier. The final order is the hardest kind: a quantity the child chooses from two candidates on the dock, where only one of them can meet the stated rules — they must pick and then build. Escalate from one rule to two rules to a choice of quantity. Keep decisions dense; no long dialogue. End the shift with the harbor master reading back the child's own refusals aloud as the proudest part of the night — refusing an impossible order is what a real packer does. Do not certify mastery in the ending text; the shift ends, the tally is shown, and the record goes to the harbor log. Assignment: Festival Team Challenge. Academic construct to preserve: Lab Learner transfers equal-groups, missing-factor, and word-problem interpretation to unseen material at high accuracy, and the uniqueness misconception observed at baseline ("only one pair") has resolved for generation: given a product, Lab Learner now produces alternative valid factor pairs without stalling. What remains untested is the negative case and the multi-constraint case. Prediction: when two constraints must hold at once, Lab Learner will satisfy the more salient rule first and check the second only after building; and when an arrangement is genuinely impossible, Lab Learner will exhaust several near-miss arrangements before considering refusal, and may ship an uneven arrangement rather than assert impossibility — because impossibility has never been modeled as a legitimate answer. This node must test unseen synthesis: combine the construct in a context not practised before. Author fresh items. These have already been seen and must not be reused verbatim: math.multiplication.equal_groups, math.multiplication.missing_factor, math.multiplication.word_problem_interpretation, math.multiplication.factor_pairs, math.multiplication.unseen_transfer.equal_groups, math.multiplication.unseen_transfer.missing_factor, math.multiplication.unseen_transfer.word_problem. Planner decision behind this node: The preregistered prediction (accuracy 0.70–1.00 on fresh unassisted transfer) was met: 3/3 unseen, unassisted, independent-probe items correct at 100%, so the transfer claim is supported at the Quest evidence limit. But the theory's specific misconception clause was not upheld — it predicted stalling and repetition when a second arrangement was demanded, and the Shape-Shifting Crate produced a re-grouping of 24 as 6 groups of 4 alongside a constrained missing-factor solve with no stall and no frustration in 75s. The uniqueness misconception therefore looks resolved on the transfer items, though the original baseline error ("only one pair") was never directly re-tested with an impossibility judgment: Lab Learner has never been observed declaring an arrangement impossible, only producing ones that work. So the hypothesis is revised rather than supported outright. Boss eligibility is satisfied on fresh, correct, unassisted Quest evidence, so the next instrument is unseen synthesis: hold several constraints at once, decide which products can satisfy them and which cannot, and defend the impossible case. Boss ends awaiting calibration; it cannot certify mastery. Created at: 2026-08-08T16:26:29.469Z.

Approved design artifact is the creative authority for presentation and interaction. Implement it faithfully; it cannot change the Planner's academic contract.
The first action, core interaction, mathematics-as-power, visible consequences, progression, world reaction, and payoff must exist as child-visible mechanics. Do not collapse the artifact into answer buttons, a question card, decorative artwork, or a progress bar.

{
  "artifactId": "boss-impossible-order-harbor-night-v1",
  "nodeId": "boss",
  "academicContractHash": "f6d7c531ed16b68f59161ce663b5e1a44a5a80cfccbd425b2e664352ff79c381",
  "title": "The Impossible Order",
  "audienceRationale": "For a 9-year-old, third grade, with fresh unassisted 3/3 transfer evidence on equal groups, missing factor, and word-problem interpretation, and a resolved-looking uniqueness misconception that has never been tested against impossibility. The design speaks in concrete physical language (fish, crates, rows) rather than symbolic notation; every constraint is checkable by eye via badges; reading load is minimal (orders are under 12 words). The night-shift-alone framing grants the grown-up responsibility 9-year-olds crave, and the harbor master praising refusals directly targets the untested construct: making \\\"no arrangement exists\\\" feel like competence, not failure. Numbers stay within 12–32, inside grade-3 fact range, so all cognitive budget goes to constraint synthesis and impossibility judgment — the actual boss skill — not fact retrieval.",
  "openingPromise": "It is your first night shift alone in the Harbor Packing House. Order slips slide in on a rattling brass conveyor, each stamped with a fish count and packing rules. Real packers ship what can be packed — and refuse what cannot. Your stamp, your stock, your call. The harbor log remembers everything.",
  "firstThreeSeconds": "The screen opens already inside the packing house: rain streaks the window, a lantern swings, and the conveyor is ALREADY moving — a paper order slip slides in with a soft mechanical clack and unrolls itself center-screen: \"PACK 12 FISH — EXACTLY 3 FISH PER ROW.\" Below it, a wooden grid crate waits, a glinting pile of silver fish sits in the stock bin at the left, and a fish is gently pulsing, begging to be dragged. Two big stamps sit at the bottom: green SHIP IT, red CANNOT BE PACKED. No menu, no instructions screen — the shift has begun.",
  "firstAction": "Drag one fish from the stock bin into the crate grid. It snaps into the top-left cell with a wet slap sound and the row outline lights up showing \"1 of 3 in this row.\" Two more drags complete the row and it locks with a satisfying wooden CLUNK, the row turning ice-blue. The child immediately understands the whole physical grammar of the game — fish fill rows, complete rows lock, and the crate is being built toward the order — before a single word of tutorial is spoken.",
  "interactionDemonstration": "Order 4 walkthrough: slip reads \"PACK 24 — MORE THAN 2 ROWS ✚ FEWER THAN 6 PER ROW.\" Child, following salience, drags fish into rows of 6 (the familiar 4×6). As the fourth row locks, the count badge goes gold (24 ✓) and the rows badge goes gold (4 rows > 2 ✓) — but the per-row badge stays grey with a small \"6 is not fewer than 6\" tooltip when tapped. SHIP IT remains dim. Child drags a fish out of the top row; the row unlocks and glows red. They tear down to rows of 4: six rows lock one by one — CLUNK, CLUNK — and on the sixth, all three badges flare gold simultaneously, SHIP IT ignites green, the child slams it, the crate lid drops, a nail-gun triple-tap seals it, and the conveyor carries it out into the night as the stock counter holds steady and the log gains a green entry. The math (24 = 6×4 but not 4×6 under these rules) was the entire mechanism of the moment.",
  "coreInteraction": "The child reads each order (a product plus one or two simultaneous structural constraints), then physically builds a rectangular array by dragging fish from a finite shared stock into a crate grid. The grid enforces mathematical structure: only complete equal rows lock (locked rows glow ice-blue); a partial or uneven row glows red, wobbles, and will not lock, and the SHIP IT stamp stays dim while any red exists. A live counter shows fish placed vs. fish ordered, and constraint badges on the order slip flip from grey to gold as each rule is currently satisfied — so the child can SEE that \"rows of 3 ✓\" is met while \"more than 4 rows ✗\" is not, forcing them to hold both constraints at once. When the child believes the arrangement meets the order, they slam SHIP IT. When they conclude no arrangement can exist, they slam CANNOT BE PACKED and must pick one justification from three short reasons (\"nothing divides it evenly,\" \"the rows don't come out even,\" \"the rule breaks the count\"); picking the right reason is part of being correct. Fish return to stock instantly on drag-out, so restructuring an attempt (tearing down 3×6 to try 6×3 or 2×9) is fast and frictionless — near-miss exploration is cheap, but shipping or refusing is a committed, stock-changing act.",
  "mathAsPower": "Multiplication IS the machine. The crate grid is a physical factor-pair engine: rows × fish-per-row must equal the ordered product, and the crate literally will not close otherwise. Every mathematical fact has a visible mechanical consequence — 17 fish in rows of more than one leaves a red, wobbling, unlockable stub row no matter how the child rearranges, making primality something you can feel with your hands; 25 in exactly 4 rows always strands one fish flashing red because 4 does not divide 25. Solving a missing factor (order says \"rows of 6\" for 24 fish) is answered by BUILDING the four rows, not by typing a number. Constraint synthesis is spatial: \"more than 4 rows AND more than 4 per row\" for 24 kills 6×4 and 4×6 visibly — gold badges refuse to both light — so the child must reason there is no factor pair of 24 with both factors above 4, and stamp the refusal. Stock arithmetic runs underneath: wrong shipments and refused-fillable orders drain a real counted supply, so multiplication and subtraction together decide whether the late-shift big order can even be attempted. Math changes the world; the world never accepts non-math.",
  "stakes": "The night's fish stock is finite and shared across every order (starting stock: 60 fish, shown as a real drawn pile that visibly shrinks). Ship a WRONG order and the inspection crane hoists the crate, the bottom drops, and every fish in it splashes into the black harbor water — gone from the shift forever. Refuse a FILLABLE order and the captain snorts, snatches their promised crate of bonus stock, and stomps off the dock — stock you will never receive. Late in the shift, the Festival Team Challenge order arrives: a big order that can only be filled if the child protected their stock with correct decisions earlier. Every stamp is therefore a bet placed with real, countable resources the child can see dwindling.",
  "consequences": "Wrong SHIP: the crane-dunk animation plays (2.5s, dramatic but not mocking), the exact spilled count floats up in red (\"−15 fish\"), and the stock pile visibly shrinks; the order slip returns stamped \"REJECTED BY INSPECTOR — count the rows\" so the child sees WHY (e.g., a row of 5 in a rows-of-4 order is circled in red). Wrong REFUSAL of a fillable order: a 3-second ghost overlay shows the arrangement that would have worked (e.g., \"4 rows of 7 fit the rules\") building itself in pale blue in the empty crate, then the captain leaves with the bonus crate (\"−10 promised fish\"). Wrong REASON on a correct refusal: half credit — the stamp holds, but the harbor master scrawls the true reason over the child's chosen one, and it counts as a flagged entry in the log. Nothing is hidden: every consequence is a visible change in stock, log, and dock.",
  "recovery": "Recovery is structural, never a lecture. After any wrong stamp, the very next order is a \"steady order\" — same constraint type, smaller product, generous margin — so the child immediately re-earns footing and a small stock rebate (\"+4 fish, dock scraps recovered\") for getting it right. Inside any single order, near-misses are free: fish drag back to stock with no penalty, and after 90 seconds of rearranging on one order the wharf cat hops onto the conveyor and paws at whichever constraint badge is being neglected (pure attention direction, no answer given). If stock ever drops below what the remaining shift needs, a \"salvage order\" appears — a genuinely fillable easy order worth bonus stock — so the shift can always be completed, though the final tally honestly records the rough night.",
  "progression": [
    "Orders 1–2 (warm hands): single-constraint fresh items — \"pack 12, exactly 3 per row\" then \"pack 21, exactly 3 rows\" (missing factor by building). Both fillable. Teaches the grid, the lock, the SHIP stamp, and the stock cost of sloppiness at low risk.",
    "Order 3 (the door opens): first genuinely impossible single-constraint order — \"pack 17 in equal rows of more than one fish.\" Every arrangement leaves a red stub. First legitimate use of CANNOT BE PACKED plus reason selection (\"nothing divides it evenly\"). This is the moment refusal is modeled as a real answer.",
    "Orders 4–5 (two rules at once): dual-constraint fillable orders — \"pack 24, more than 2 rows AND fewer than 6 fish per row\" (4×6 fails a rule, 6×4 works — the salience trap made visible by the gold badges), then \"pack 30, an even number of rows AND more than 4 per row.\"",
    "Order 6 (two rules, no exit): dual-constraint impossible — \"pack 25 in exactly 4 equal rows\" or \"pack 24 with more than 4 rows AND more than 4 per row.\" The child must exhaust or reason past near-misses and stamp refusal with the right reason (\"the rule breaks the count\").",
    "Order 7 (the squeeze): the stock-pressure order — a large fillable order (e.g., \"pack 28, exactly 4 rows\") that is only affordable if earlier stock was protected; if stock is short, the salvage-order path opens first. Makes earlier decisions retroactively meaningful.",
    "Order 8 (final — choose then build): the Festival Team Challenge order. Two candidate crates sit on the dock — e.g., 32 fish and 27 fish — under the rule \"equal rows of exactly 8.\" Only one candidate can obey the rule. The child must first CHOOSE the quantity (committing the other crate back to the boat), then build it correctly. Choosing wrong strands them with an impossible build they must then refuse — recoverable but costly. This is full synthesis: judge two products against constraints before touching a single fish.",
    "Shift end: the harbor master reads the log aloud, and reads the child's REFUSALS proudest of all — \"Order 3: refused. Reason: nothing divides seventeen evenly. That's a packer's eye, that is.\" Tally shown (shipped, refused, spilled, stock remaining). No mastery language; the record is stamped and slid into the harbor log drawer, awaiting the harbor master's morning review."
  ],
  "interactionContinuity": "One continuous shift, one continuous interaction grammar. The drag-build-lock-stamp loop established in the first ten seconds never changes; only the orders deepen (one rule → two rules → impossibility → stock squeeze → choose-then-build). The conveyor is the sole scene-transition device — orders slide in, crates slide out — so there are no menus, cutscenes, or mode switches anywhere in the experience. Stock, log, and dock persist visibly across all eight orders, making every decision feel like part of one accumulating night rather than a sequence of disconnected problems. The final choose-then-build order uses the identical grid and stamps; only the judgment demanded has grown.",
  "worldReaction": "The world answers every mathematical act physically. Correct rows lock with a wooden clunk and ice-blue glow; illegal rows wobble red and refuse. Correct shipments: lid slams, nails fire, the crate rides the conveyor out, a distant boat horn approves, the harbor log gains a green stamped line. Correct refusals: the red seal thuds down, the order slip is spiked on the refusal spike with the chosen reason printed on it, and the harbor master's silhouette at the office window gives a slow nod. Wrong shipments: crane hoist, trapdoor, splash, gulls scatter, stock pile visibly craters. Wrong refusals: the ghost-array builds itself in pale blue as silent proof, and the captain marches off with the bonus crate. The dock itself keeps score — spiked refusals, stacked shipped crates, and floating debris from spills are all persistently visible set dressing that the child's math has authored.",
  "payoff": "The shift-end scene: lanterns dim, the conveyor stops, and the harbor master walks the dock reading the night's log aloud in a gravelly, warm voice-line style (text with audio sting). Shipments get a nod — but the refusals get the ceremony: each spiked refusal slip is held up to the lantern and read with the child's chosen reason (\"Seventeen. Nothing divides it evenly. Correct call.\"), because refusing an impossible order is what a real packer does. The full tally appears as a stamped ledger page — orders shipped, orders refused, fish spilled, fish remaining — and the page slides into the harbor log drawer with a final stamp: \"RECORDED. AWAITING HARBOR MASTER'S MORNING REVIEW.\" No mastery is certified; the night simply ends with the child's judgment on the record, and the Festival Team Challenge crate (if earned) sits gleaming on the dock for the team.",
  "replayVariation": "On replay the order generator reshuffles products and constraints from a fresh-item pool (products 12–36; constraint templates: exact rows, exact per-row, inequality on rows, inequality on per-row, parity of rows, dual inequalities), guaranteeing at least two genuinely impossible orders per shift in new positions so refusal timing can't be memorized. The final choose-then-build candidates change (e.g., 30 vs 26 under \"equal rows of exactly 5\"). Starting stock and salvage thresholds shift slightly to change the economic texture. A returning child also unlocks \"foreman mode\" flavor: one order per shift arrives with a smudged number the child must infer from a stated rule plus the visible crate size — same construct, higher inference — keeping the same eight-order shape but never the same night twice.",
  "visualDirection": "Warm-lantern-against-cold-night palette: deep indigo harbor and rain outside the window; amber lamplight pooling on worn wooden planks inside. Fish are chunky, satisfying silver-blue sprites with a slight wet sheen and squash-and-stretch on pickup. The crate grid is honest carpentry — visible nail heads, rope handles — with locked rows glowing calm ice-blue and illegal rows pulsing warning red with a subtle wobble. Order slips are cream paper with big stamped numerals and two constraint badges that flip grey→gold when satisfied; typography is large, high-contrast, readable by a 9-year-old at a glance. The stock pile is drawn as a literal heap that shrinks in visible chunks. Stamps are oversized rubber stamps with ink texture; the refusal stamp leaves a proud red seal, not a shameful X. Everything readable in one screen, no scrolling, decision surface always visible.",
  "motionDirection": "Motion is weighty and dockside-mechanical: fish squash on grab and slap-settle into cells; rows lock with a short compression bounce; the conveyor moves with a rhythmic tick-advance rather than smooth glide. The red illegal-row wobble is a small ±2° oscillation — noticeable, never seizure-adjacent. Stamps descend with anticipation (brief hover, then thump with a 4-frame ink splash). The crane-dunk is the biggest animation in the game (hoist, pause, trapdoor, splash, gull scatter) and is reserved exclusively for wrong shipments so its drama carries meaning. Ghost-array builds animate row by row at readable speed (~350ms per row). All motion uses ease-out timing under 400ms except the two ceremony moments (dunk, shift-end reading); nothing animates during the child's active reasoning except the gentle badge glow, keeping the thinking surface calm.",
  "soundDirection": "Ambient bed: soft rain on the roof, creaking timbers, distant buoy bell, low harbor water lap — loopable, unobtrusive, mixable under thought. Interaction foley: wet slap on fish placement, deep wooden CLUNK on row lock (the game's signature satisfaction sound), papery slide-clack for arriving orders, heavy rubber thud + ink squish for stamps. Success shipment: nail-gun triple-tap, conveyor rumble, distant approving boat horn. Wrong shipment: crane chain rattle, hollow trapdoor bang, big splash, gull cries — dramatic, never a mocking failure jingle. Refusal seal: a proud, resonant thud distinct from the ship stamp, slightly lower in pitch, so refusal sounds authoritative. Shift-end: rain fades, a single warm accordion phrase under the harbor master's reading. No background music during active problem-solving; the sound design lets the child hear their own decisions land.",
  "usefulLibraries": [
    "PixiJS (2D WebGL sprite rendering for fish, crate grid, conveyor, water)",
    "GSAP (stamp thumps, crane-dunk sequence, badge flips, ghost-array builds)",
    "Howler.js (layered ambient bed + interaction foley with per-channel volume)",
    "@dnd-kit or interact.js (accessible pointer/touch drag of fish into grid cells)",
    "seedrandom (deterministic per-shift order generation for replay variation and evidence reproducibility)"
  ],
  "engagementPrediction": "Prior evidence shows this child rates construction-style, self-paced activities highest (5s with replay on construction and adapted routes) and abandoned the speed-pressure route (2). This design is therefore hands-on building with zero timers — pressure comes from resource scarcity and judgment, not clocks. Predicted engagement: high; the drag-build loop matches their demonstrated construction appetite, the stock economy gives the paced tension they tolerated well, and the refusal stamp offers a novel power move. Predicted friction point: Order 3 (first impossible order) may produce 60–120s of near-miss rearranging before the first refusal, exactly as the Planner prediction anticipates — this is the instrument working, not disengagement, and the free drag-back plus cat nudge keep it from tipping into frustration. Falsification signal: abandonment or three consecutive wrong stamps without rearrangement attempts.",
  "falsifyingEvidence": "The design's instrument claims are falsified if: (1) the child ships an uneven/red arrangement path never occurs because the grid blocks it — so instead the falsifiable behavioral signal is stamping CANNOT BE PACKED on fillable orders more than twice without any rearrangement attempts, indicating refusal is being used as an escape hatch rather than a judgment (instrument failure: refusal too cheap); (2) the child solves impossible orders by immediate refusal with correct reasons but ALSO refuses fillable dual-constraint orders at >40% rate, indicating the two-constraint load exceeds capacity and the boss is measuring overload, not synthesis; (3) engagement collapse (abandonment, or >3 minutes idle) at Order 3, indicating impossibility-as-answer was not adequately legitimized by the design; (4) the Planner's prediction (satisfy salient rule first, check second after building) fails to appear even once across dual-constraint orders — which would suggest the badges telegraph the second constraint so strongly that the boss cannot observe the predicted behavior, weakening its diagnostic value. Any of these routes the artifact back for revision rather than to calibration."
}


The Planner's design decisions for this node. Build these; do not soften them:
- Core interaction: The child drags fish one at a time or in a swipe from a stock bin into a rectangular pen. Fish snap into rows left to right. A row that is not full stays translucent and pulses red; the pen will not lock while any row is incomplete. As fish land, a live readout under the pen updates — "4 rows × 5 fish = 20" — and turns green only when both stated rules are satisfied simultaneously. Pressing SHIP IT with a red readout tips the pen sideways: the fish slide out, splash, and the stock counter drops by that amount with an audible fall — they do not come back. Pressing CANNOT BE PACKED shows a stamp thudding onto the order; if the order was truly impossible, the harbor master nods and the order pins to the log board; if it was packable, the captain's boat pulls away with the crate still aboard and the log board shows an empty slot. On screen, failure looks like an emptying stock bin and a log board with holes in it.
- What is at risk: Fish stock is finite and non-renewable within the shift. Every wrong ship spills a crate into the harbor and permanently shrinks the supply the child has for later orders; every wrong refusal loses a paying captain and their crate. Because a late order requires stock the child must still have, early carelessness makes a later order literally unfillable — the child watches an order they understand perfectly slide past because they no longer have the fish. What is at risk is the completeness of the night's manifest, and the child can end the shift with a short, visibly incomplete log that is theirs.
- How a run goes wrong: The shift can be failed. If stock drops below what the remaining orders need, orders start sliding off the conveyor unfilled, and the shift ends early with the harbor log short and gaps marked in it. The two distinct failures are readable and separate: forcing an uneven arrangement through and shipping it (spilled crate) versus stamping CANNOT BE PACKED on an order that was in fact packable (lost captain). Both are recorded by name in the log, so the child sees which mistake was theirs.
- How pressure builds: Order one is a single rule with an obvious answer, ten seconds, one solution. Orders two through four add a second simultaneous rule so satisfying only one is now a visible failure. Order five is the first genuine impossibility, arriving with no warning among fillable orders so the child must notice it themselves. Orders six through eight mix fillable and impossible unpredictably while stock is already reduced, and the conveyor speed increases slightly so hesitation costs an order. The final order requires the child to choose which of two quantities on the dock can satisfy the rules, refuse the other, and then build the array from remaining stock.
- The mathematical hook to make visible: Some numbers are generous and some are stubborn. Twenty-four will rearrange itself into rows of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, or 12 for anyone who asks — but 17 will not break into equal rows at all, no matter how the fish are pushed around, and no amount of trying changes that. The whoa is discovering that "it can't be done" is a real mathematical answer with a reason behind it, and that saying so out loud is a stronger move than forcing a row that doesn't fit.
If the Planner specified a way to fail, that failure must be genuinely reachable on screen and must cost the child something they can see. Do not replace it with a hint, a retry, or an encouraging message.

Never display the answer to a question before the child has committed to a response.

Author fresh content appropriate to this assignment and node responsibility. Do not reuse any exposed item identity or exact prompt listed in the cycle. Quest must test unseen transfer. Boss must test unseen synthesis. A generated support node remains teaching/practice evidence. Do not claim mastery.
The first visible H1 must be exactly "The Impossible Order". A short exciting subtitle may establish the AI-authored world.
Visibly use the assigned artwork URL as part of the world: none.
Keep the complete HTML under 24,000 characters. Prefer concise CSS and JavaScript.
Every DOM element queried by JavaScript must exist before the query runs; place behavior after its markup or initialize it on DOMContentLoaded.

Runtime contract appendix:
Load <script src="/games/_contract.js"></script> in <head>.
Read runtime identity and parameters from window.GAME_PARAMS. Never hardcode the child identity, homework identity, or session identity into the HTML.
Emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"activity_ready",payload:{nodeId:"boss"}},"*") when ready.
Whenever the activity or problem changes, emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"game_state_update",payload:{game:"generated-math",activityId:"boss",nodeId:"boss",phase:"question",activityTitle:"The Impossible Order",learningFocus:"math.multiplication.synthesis.constrained_factor_pairs_and_impossibility — given a product and two simultaneous structural constraints, generate a valid rectangular arrangement, solve for an unknown factor, or correctly determine that no arrangement exists and justify why.",mechanic:"Drag-to-pack rectangular array building against written shipping orders, with a limited stock of crates, a commit button, and a refusal stamp that is sometimes the only correct answer.",currentChallenge,availableActions,itemIndex,totalItems,answerVisibility:"hidden"}},"*") so Elli has live context. Never expose answers.
Represent currentChallenge as {id,prompt,mode,readAloudRequested:false,readAloudCount}. When the child activates a visible Read it to me control, increment readAloudCount and resend that same answer-hidden state with readAloudRequested:true. Do not narrate it inside the activity.
Listen for parent messages with type:"sunny_companion_presence". Pause activity timers and input while summoned, and resume the same state when collapsed. Do not restart or change progress.
Maintain a factual targetResults array. For every submitted answer append {target,correct,attemptedValue,responseTimeMs,scaffoldLevel} using a stable fresh item identity.
For every answer call window.fireAttemptEvent({domain:"math",target,correct,attemptedValue,responseTimeMs,scaffoldLevel}).
Emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"progress_event",payload:{nodeId:"boss",completedItems,totalItems}},"*") whenever visible progress advances.
Use window.fireCompanionEvent("correct_answer" or "wrong_answer", {target}) after meaningful answers and window.fireCompanionEvent("game_complete", {}) at completion.
On completion calculate accuracy from targetResults and call window.sendNodeComplete({nodeId:window.GAME_PARAMS.nodeId,completed:true,accuracy,targetResults,timeSpent_ms}).
Expose window.SUNNY_VALIDATION_HOOKS = {playthrough: async () => { ... }}. This is required for Quest and Boss. The hook must use the same handlers as visible child controls, exercise an incorrect response and visible recovery, complete every assessable item, and reach completion. It must not fabricate or post evidence directly.
Include <div id="sunny-companion"></div>; Sunny owns its rendering, so do not create companion chrome. Return raw HTML only and end with </html>.

  "design": {
    "stakes": "Fish stock is finite and non-renewable within the shift. Every wrong ship spills a crate into the harbor and permanently shrinks the supply the child has for later orders; every wrong refusal loses a paying captain and their crate. Because a late order requires stock the child must still have, early carelessness makes a later order literally unfillable — the child watches an order they understand perfectly slide past because they no longer have the fish. What is at risk is the completeness of the night's manifest, and the child can end the shift with a short, visibly incomplete log that is theirs.",
    "failureMode": "The shift can be failed. If stock drops below what the remaining orders need, orders start sliding off the conveyor unfilled, and the shift ends early with the harbor log short and gaps marked in it. The two distinct failures are readable and separate: forcing an uneven arrangement through and shipping it (spilled crate) versus stamping CANNOT BE PACKED on an order that was in fact packable (lost captain). Both are recorded by name in the log, so the child sees which mistake was theirs.",
    "escalation": "Order one is a single rule with an obvious answer, ten seconds, one solution. Orders six through eight mix fillable and impossible unpredictably while stock is already reduced, and the conveyor speed increases slightly so hesitation costs an order. The final order requires the child to choose which of two quantities on the dock can satisfy the rules, refuse the other, and then build the array from remaining stock.",
    "mechanicSpec": "The child drags fish one at a time or in a swipe from a stock bin into a rectangular pen. Fish snap into rows left to right. As fish land, a live readout under the pen updates — \"4 rows × 5 fish = 20\" — and turns green only when both stated rules are satisfied simultaneously. Pressing SHIP IT with a red readout tips the pen sideways: the fish slide out, splash, and the stock counter drops by that amount with an audible fall — they do not come back. Pressing CANNOT BE PACKED shows a stamp thudding onto the order; if the order was truly impossible, the harbor master nods and the order pins to the log board; if it was packable, the captain's boat pulls away with the crate still aboard and the log board shows an empty slot. On screen, failure looks like an emptying stock bin and a log board with holes in it.",
